subject: math
description: Students display numerical data sets on a number line using dot plots (line plots), histograms, and box plots. They must read a data set or frequency information, choose or build the requested display, place data correctly (one dot per value, data binned into equal-width intervals for histograms, and the five-number summary $\min, Q_1, \text{median}, Q_3, \max$ for box plots), and read values back out of a given display. They also recognize which display fits a question and interpret features such as frequency, intervals, and quartiles.
subSkills: Build a dot plot from a raw data list (one dot per data value, correctly scaled number line)
Read frequencies and individual values back out of a dot plot
Group data into equal-width intervals (bins) and build a histogram, choosing a sensible bin width
Read frequencies and interval membership out of a histogram (and recognize that individual values are not recoverable)
Order data and compute the five-number summary: $\min$, lower quartile $Q_1$, median, upper quartile $Q_3$, $\max$
Construct a box plot from the five-number summary and compute the interquartile range $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$
Read the five-number summary and IQR back out of a given box plot
Match a data set or question to the appropriate display type

problemArchetypes.name: Build a dot plot
problemArchetypes.example: The number of pets owned by $12$ students is $0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 1, 0, 2, 4$. Describe the dot plot: how many dots sit above each value $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ on the number line.

problemArchetypes.name: Read a dot plot
problemArchetypes.example: A dot plot of daily absences shows dots above $0$ (4 dots), $1$ (3 dots), $2$ (2 dots), and $5$ (1 dot). How many days are recorded, and on how many days were there at least $2$ absences?

problemArchetypes.name: Build a histogram from intervals
problemArchetypes.example: Plant heights in cm are $4, 7, 9, 11, 12, 14, 18, 19, 21, 23$. Using equal-width intervals of width $5$ starting at $0$ ($0\text{–}4$, $5\text{–}9$, $10\text{–}14$, $15\text{–}19$, $20\text{–}24$), give the frequency (bar height) for each interval.

problemArchetypes.name: Read a histogram
problemArchetypes.example: A histogram of test scores has intervals $50\text{–}59$ (height $2$), $60\text{–}69$ (height $5$), $70\text{–}79$ (height $8$), $80\text{–}89$ (height $4$), $90\text{–}99$ (height $1$). How many students scored at least $70$? Can you tell exactly how many scored $73$?

problemArchetypes.name: Five-number summary and box plot
problemArchetypes.example: Order the data $7, 3, 9, 5, 11, 8, 6, 10, 4$ and find $\min$, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, and $\max$. Then describe the box plot and compute the $\text{IQR}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Read a box plot
problemArchetypes.example: A box plot of quiz scores has $\min = 4$, $Q_1 = 7$, median $= 10$, $Q_3 = 13$, $\max = 18$. What is the $\text{IQR}$, and what fraction of the data lies between $7$ and $13$?

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the right display
problemArchetypes.example: You want to show how $200$ commute times group into ranges without listing every value. Which display (dot plot, histogram, or box plot) is most appropriate, and why?

Easy.description: Single display, small clean data set or a fully labeled display already given. Reading or building a dot plot, reading a histogram's bar heights, or reading a five-number summary straight off a box plot. One step, no quartile computation, no binning decisions.
constraints: Data set has $\le 12$ values, all small non-negative integers
For dot plots: build or count dots, one dot per value
For histograms: intervals and bar heights are given; only read frequencies
For box plots: the five-number summary is given; only read a value or count what fraction lies in a region
No computation of $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, or IQR required

Medium.description: One full construction step. Bin a data set into given equal-width intervals to get histogram heights, OR order a data set and compute the median and quartiles for a box plot, OR compute the IQR from a five-number summary. Data sets are larger and may need ordering first.
constraints: Data set has $12$ to $20$ values, may be unordered
Histogram: interval width and start are given; student assigns each value to a bin and counts
Box plot: student orders the data, then finds median, $Q_1$, $Q_3$ (odd or even count), and $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$
Quartiles fall on integer or half-integer values requiring averaging two middle numbers

Hard.description: Multi-step or judgment required. Choose an appropriate bin width and build the histogram from scratch, OR compute the full five-number summary AND interpret it (compare two box plots, reason about spread), OR decide which of the three displays fits a scenario and justify it, OR convert information between displays.
constraints: Student must choose a reasonable interval width (not given) and justify the number of bins
Comparison of two distributions via two box plots or two histograms (which has greater spread / IQR / median)
Reason about what a display can and cannot show (e.g., a histogram hides individual values)
Data set has $\ge 20$ values or includes a value that affects the quartile boundaries
May ask student to select the correct display and explain the choice

difficultyRubric._tierSplit: This standard spans three distinct display types, so it warrants the two-worksheet split. tier1 (Easy to Medium) covers dot plots and histograms: building and reading dot plots, then binning data and reading/building histograms. tier2 (Medium to Hard) covers box plots and synthesis: the five-number summary, IQR, constructing and reading box plots, comparing distributions, and choosing the appropriate display. The single ramped worksheet, if used instead, runs dot plots (Easy) to histograms (Easy/Medium) to box plots and quartiles (Medium) to display-choice and comparison (Hard).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a histogram like a bar graph and leaves gaps or uses unequal-width intervals
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reads or builds bars over single discrete values or with mismatched interval widths instead of equal-width contiguous bins

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks individual data values can be recovered from a histogram
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims to know exactly how many scored $73$ from an interval $70\text{–}79$ of height $8$, e.g., answers $8$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student forgets to order the data before finding the median and quartiles
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Takes the middle of the unordered list as the median, e.g., calls the $5$th listed value the median without sorting

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student finds the median by averaging the first and last value instead of the middle
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes $\frac{\min + \max}{2}$ and calls it the median, e.g., $\frac{3 + 11}{2} = 7$ for $3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11$ instead of the true median $7$ from the middle position

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student computes the range instead of the IQR
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives $\max - \min$ instead of $Q_3 - Q_1$, e.g., reports $18 - 4 = 14$ when the IQR is $13 - 7 = 6$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student miscounts a dot plot by counting stacked dots as a single value or skipping empty values on the number line
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the total number of distinct values instead of the total number of dots, e.g., answers $4$ for a plot with dots above $0,1,2,5$ rather than the $10$ data points

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student swaps $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ or places the median outside the box
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Builds a box plot with $Q_3 < Q_1$ or with the median line outside the box, giving a negative IQR such as $7 - 13 = -6$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses the wrong display for the question
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a dot plot to summarize $200$ values into ranges, or a box plot to show every individual value, instead of a histogram
